projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Jack Houghtlin was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: 1941, on Division Avenue in what we called the projects; a new apartment housing development from the Government. I went in in January of 1941. I was drafted. I went to Camp Shelby, Mississippi with the 37th Division, 112th Combat Engineer Regiment.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any interesting or unusual stories from basic training?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: We spent a good deal of our basic in Louisiana on manuevers. The first six weeks we spent going to the Leaf River building a bridge approach. In the afternoon the Company went out and blew it up. But our turn would come. The next day they went out and built it, we went out and blew it up. Shelby was a nice post. It was an old post.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you first went into the Army was it tough being thrown in there with guys from all over the country? A tough adjustment?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Not really. I came directly out of the Three Cs; Civilian Conservation Corp. I had been stationed in Defiane, Ohio, which is south of Toledo. When I got my notice they were nice about it. They gave me leave so I could go home and sign up. I had spent the previous six months to going into Three Cs trying to enter the service. For the Navy I had too much overbite. For the Marines I didn't weigh enough. For the Army they found something. But when I got my draft notice I begin to wonder would I pass with flying colors? So, we were in Camp Shelby in January of '41. In January of '42 we lost the continental limits of the United States, wound up in Ireland. Spent a year in Ireland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was that crossing like when you crossed the Atlantic?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Cold and miserable. North Atlantic is not a place to be in the middle of the winter. We left on the Chateau Thierry (ph). We had half of a Regiment. A Regiment is about, between 1100 and 1200 men. So, we had 5- or 600 men aboard the Chateau Thierry (ph). It's 300 foot long, 52 feet abeam, draws about 22 foot of water. There were times when the swells on the ocean surrounded the Chateau Thierry (ph). The only place to look was up. Other than that it was water. The pumps run continually. We shut them off twice on the way across due to the submarine alert. That's the only times they were turned off.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You didn't have any close calls with any ?U-boots?, though, right?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Not that I'm aware of, other than two times the pumps were shut off because of an alert. That doesn't give us any idea where they were; how close, how far. But it run pretty well. We had an air alert a couple of times and they put a gunnery crew up on top. There were 14 of us up there. They enclosed and topped the hatchway from the engine room. When you were off duty you could rest on the hot glass on the top of the airway. But we were approached once after we got closer to Ireland. We had no idea where we were going but it seemed to be taking quite a while to get there. We left the continental limits on the 15th of January and arrived in ____, Ireland on the 26th. So, we were 11 days crossing. But we were approached, as I say, once by a British aircraft who made the error of coming down in the sun to see who we were. We had Navy gunners aboard. The others were CVs who were on the ship. But the Navy gunners, and of course we tried, open fire on the aircraft. It's a good thing we didn't hit it. But that was the last time we were approached in that manner. But other than that it was fairly quiet. Our bunk room was stacked six high. It was good to get up on the deck as part of the gunnery crew. Our arrival in Ireland we disembarked, we marched so far. We went to Londonderry, Ireland. And from there we marched up to our barracks. We were in, oh, maybe 12, 13 different towns in Ireland. We put up three or four storage depots for supplies in Valley Clare (ph), _____ , several other places.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your particular job with the outfit?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: When I started I was a truck driver. I drove a ton and a half. After we was there for a while I drove most anything. We had an RD-6 bulldozer, a Diamond T and trailer, command car, five or six jeeps, the rest were all ton and a halfs.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was life like in Ireland there in '42?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Very quiet except for training. Very quiet. The people were fine. We got passes to go to town, not that all fire many of them; but we did get to go to town. We had a fairly large depot at Valley Clare (ph). We had one that was full of lumber in another town; Moneymar (ph), I think. As I say, we put up Iris and ?Nissan? huts; double Nissan. Poured concrete. Used to wonder why they were so particular about where they went until we found out that you couldn't put two huts on one man's property. You had to put one on his and one on his neighbors.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was the rules they had agreed to?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Yes. So when we left everyone had a new barn, good barns. Some of them I guess are still there. But I never went back. A lot of the fellas made return trips, but we didn't. I didn't do that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have many air raids there where you were?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: We had our share. Nothing that close to us. After we got to England we had more. We were in England, we were about, oh, maybe 50 miles from London to Deviasis. We were surrounded by Air Force bases, but I don't seem to recall that many air raids. London was getting them. England's east coast on the channel was getting them. But we didn't seem to have too many our way. Of course, like I say, we are about 50-miles west of London. I think the closest town to us was Bath. And it was about maybe 20, 22-miles to Bath. But a lot of training, a lot of marching, a lot of schools.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of things were you going to school for?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Demolition, building water crossings, pontoon boats, treadway bridges, walking bridges, things like that. We started out with dynamite, graduated to plastique, and went up from there. But it was interesting.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were there any practice invasions, anything like that, practicing on the coast?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: We built at -- sure -- New Quay, outside of New Quay we built an assault practice landing affair. Shortly after it was finished we lost, not my unit, but U.S. lost about 7, 800 men at that landing, practice landing. The Germans watched the landing ships come up the channel and go in. And when they came in they used what we called PT boats, they used to come across and wreak all the havoc they could. And they killed about, between 7- and 800 people, troops.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you know about that at the time or did you learn about that later?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: We found out about that later.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Because after we built it we didn't try it out. We moved on. We spent most of our time strictly engineer work; mine fields -- after the landings, mine fields, putting them down, taking them up, clearing roadways, fixing them, little items. I understand we built the biggest land mine range that was laid in Germany, but I did not spend much time there. The invasion was on the 6th and on the 19th I was out of there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did you go in on D-Day?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Yes, the unit was amongst the first in. Primary interest: Clear the beach of land mines and other so-called dangerous items. 146th was in the water doing the same thing to the approach of Omaha Beach. They cleared the water obstacles. That was their primary. Ours was the beach itself.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How early did you go in?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Invasion started at 6:30. I think the first troops out of the 112th were there about 6:31; followed rather closely by the Big Red One and the 29th. We lost 12 men in a hurry. We suffered 22, 22 or 25 seriously wounded that were removed from the beach as soon as possible.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How big was the battalion at that point?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Three letter companies headquarters and Cirius Company and headquarters. At that time we were part of the 1121st Engineer Group; 112th, 107th, 146th, and I think it was the 108th. I wouldn't swear to that. 107th was a Michigan outfit. When we first got to Ireland and the ship burned at the dock in the states we acquired the 107th Combat Engineer Battalion and we became a regiment again. 112th had the senior time so they kept the 112th number. We were a battalion for about, until around June of '43 and they broke us up again when the 1121st was formed. We had the 112th, the 254th, the 107th, and they brought in, I'm pretty sure it was the 108th. They were a treadway bridge outfit. We trained individually, strange as it seems, as a group but ...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So were you helping to clear obstacles on D-Day then?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Beg pardon?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that part of your job on D-Day to help clear out mines, obstacles?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Your particular job?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: There were no trucks.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not at that point.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember what you were thinking when you were in there that early on D-Day?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Not much, just get the hell off of this beach. We spent a lot of time on the beach. But they finally got things cleaned up to the point where we could do what we came for, why we went to work at that. But there wasn't too much being done right at the start, but we were kept busy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else you remember from that day, from D-day?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: No, not that much.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Nothing else comes to mind?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: No. No, I'm afraid not.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Lose any bodies on that day?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We lost Sergeant Major Medgood (ph), John Medgood. We didn't loose Joe Joath (ph), got the bronze star for the landing, or a silver star for the landing. Went back out and got a buddy of his, brought him to safety. We lost our commanding officer, two lieutenants, a master sergeant, lost 10 or 12 people real quick. But we had somewhere around 20 or 22 seriously wounded. Red Zluzniak (ph). Strange after all this time the names slip.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What happened next for you then?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Oh, we moved forward and cleaned things out on the way. Thirteen days after the landing I was on my way back out of there. I have no idea what happened. I woke up two days later, came back home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were wounded then?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Yeah. I don't know what it was. They took something across my mind, forehead; and I don't remember much for the next couple of days. But before we left for overseas there were six or eight of us luckiest fellas in the world. We come home, that was in April. As we come home, I married my wife.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You married her before you went overseas?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Yeah, as far as she knows she wasn't married until I got back. I didn't stay here that long. I wasn't gone long enough for it to matter. I spent a little more time in the hospitals, then was reassigned to Fort Myers, Virginia with the 703rd MP Battalion which was nice, nice post, beautiful. Set up at the top of the hill from Arlington National Cemetery. But I could at least come home once in a while from there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were your wounds when you were wounded?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Just this (indicating).

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That crease across your forehead there?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you don't know if that was shrapnel or a bullet or what?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: It wasn't a bullet.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Probably shrapnel.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Had to be something bigger than a bullet.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Bullet, I think, would have taken me right through the top of the head.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: And if it was shrapnel I had to catch it flat and on the flat side. And caught on the edge of any of the flats would have also been dead. But it was interesting. I never had the urge to go back. I would have liked to have gone back to Ireland, but my wife had no interest in it, so I didn't go. But...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long did you, did it take you to recover from your wounds?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: I'm still going to the VA Hospital for some of the end results of those wounds, and I have been out of the service since August of '45. So, it's taken quite a while to get over some of them. We managed to have six children. We had five daughters and a son. My son retired from the Air Force ten years ago with 25 years of service. Our youngest daughter is now 40. Doesn't seem that long. But, no, I still go to the VA about every other month sometimes depending on what they are after. I have MRIs, CAT scans, things like that. They are still checking on my head. I have a mass in the back of it the MRIs picked up. All the CAT scans I had before never showed it. I have acquired Parkinsons, which doesn't help me much. But all in all I'm still here. I'll be 84 on the 18th of this month.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, happy birthday in advance.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: So, seems so -- what happened then was meant to be and meant to turn out the way it did because I'm still here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences during the war does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Not really. I'll say this much for the water in the channel, it is cold.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you pretty far out when you were let off the landing craft on the D-Day?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Our water where we come off was about waist deep, a little deeper. George Lazara (ph) was probably one of the shortest fellas in our outfit; lightweight. He used to box in Cleveland. But he come off and his lifebelt came right up under his arms. He was pulled closer to shore so he could assist in the landing. We didn't want to lose him by drowning. But fellas were in the service, we just buried one Saturday, Les Verdon (ph). About a month before that we lost Wayne Brocker (ph). You could always pick Wayne out when there was a parade at Shelby. He was a head taller than anybody else in the Unit. He was about 6-5, 6-6, somewhere in there. About broom handle-type build. Very tall. We have had a reunion for the last 59 years as close to D-Day as we can get it on a Saturday. Used to be a two-day affair. Saturday night was for adults; dinner dance, drinking. The last few it has been mostly Saturday night, no Sunday. Of course, like me, the kids I used to bring, as I say now, my youngest wasn't even there, but she's 40. Our oldest is 58. But it's been good. We have fallen off drastically. Two years ago we had 36 fellas at the reunion. Last year we had 16. We used to lose maybe 10 or 12 in a year's time. Now we loose 18 or 20. So we are down just over a hundred of us left and...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Are most of the guys from this area? From Northeast Ohio?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: We were originally. 37th was an Ohio unit and 112th was based here. Used to have their meetings in the old armory down on Lakeside. That was years ago. When it was split up we had a company in Lorain, company down around Akron. Headquarters is in Brook Park where the armory is at. We're still in contact with the 112th, per se. They somehow or another posted me for being awarded the Bronze Order of the Flurry medal, was presented to me at the reunion this year.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that an award from the French Government?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: No. That was -- the Flurry was an engineer that served with George Washington.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, Flurry, yeah, okay.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: He served with George Washington. But we are still pretty much in touch.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you were in Great Briton before D-Day was there much of a chance for entertainment? Did you catch any shows or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Oh, yeah, we had shows in Ireland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: We were Bob Hope's first entertainment.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: We were at Valley Claire, Ireland; and he stayed at the Bare (ph) Hotel. {Buzzing noise} We don't hear mention of that, but he was kept pretty busy. Is that your ride?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get a chance to meet Bob Hope or anything?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: No, we didn't meet him. We saw him, but we didn't meet him, per se.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: But --

sp.speaker: Unidentified female
sp.p: (Unintelligible)

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Oh, William?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else come to mind?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: No. Bring back memories to how many of us are gone.

sp.speaker: Unidentified female
sp.p: Tell them about the paperboy, Jack.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The paperboy.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Oh, Sid Green was our paperboy at New Quay in England. And he's been over here a couple of times. He stayed with us for a month. He retired from the British Air Force, 25 years of service.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He delivered the paper to your barracks?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: He come around and sold the paper to us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (Laughing)

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: He's out to make a buck here and there. That was Sid. Sid's still alive. He's still lives in the same place. We correspond by e-mail once in a while. His wife died sometime ago. And his biggest thing in life now is his grandson. Now his grandson must be 25, 30, somewhere in there. These times go by, God.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, you certainly weren't in France very long --

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- but was there any souvenir collecting in the outfit.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Oh, I would imagine so.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not with you, though?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: No, I didn't do much collecting. I worked. I was a powder monkey for a while.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What exactly is a powder monkey?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: You put together what they use to take down the buildings.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: And we used to be called on once in a while to make a building free so it could be entered and left without fear. And I'm not much for gathering things on the side. When I came back from overseas I kept -- I come back and we were put in Fifth General Hospital in Stanton Island New York, New York. I had a new pair of boots, two Luger, one dagger. And when I left the hospital to come to the city of Ohio via the hospital route I didn't even have a duffel bag. I came with the clothes I was wearing and that was it. Never saw the pistols or the knife again. Never saw the boots for sure. But at least I'm here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes. You said "make a building free"?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what exactly would you do to the building to make it safe to go into?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Well, you go around and find old booby traps and all the other setups --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you had to disarm those?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: -- and other items. Yes, that was one of the engineer's unheralded jobs. Mostly you hear about them building bridges. But they did do a few other things. You don't hear about them laying or clearing out mine _____+ (3 seconds) it can be. There was always the thought in the back of your mind that this one is going to go off. But you do your damndest not to think about that and concentrate on what you were taught to do and how to do it. END OF SIDE ONE, DISC ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, DISC ONE. Engineers done a lot of things. Third Battalion out of Company A was the 146th Combat Engineers and the 38th Squadron, when the Battle of the Bulge started, between the three of them they held their own well enough to be awarded the Second Presidential Unit Citation. The engineer's infantry is great. Without them I don't know what we have would have done. But you hear about the infantry, you hear about the artillery, you hear about the armored, you hear about all these outfits but you don't hear about the engineers. Nobody brings them up. And yet when the infantry and the armored were racing forward and came to a bridge, it was the engineers that went over the bridge and under the bridge and by the bridge before they ever went across it. That was to make sure they were going to get on the other side. Mine fields, like I say, we laid probably the biggest one that was laid over there; the 112th. They also took up a great number of them. That's not mentioned. I don't know if they don't like to talk about the engineers or what but...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How big was that mine field that you said was the largest?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: About 5,000 by 5,000 feet. I have no idea how many mines went in there. Usually they went in on a diagonal. In other words, if you laid them on the top of the ground they would look like a military cemetery; straight line here, here. If you look from this way it was still a straight line and a straight line. They were not laid so much this way as angled and kept up. But there was a lot of mines in a field that big.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And what was that -- why was that put up? What was it protecting?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Troops.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Troops behind there?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there any particular trick or technique to clearing a mine field to get a mine out of there?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: You pray a lot. Usually if you use a finder you could come up with them. As for getting them out, you prayed a lot. If you stepped on the trigger of one it did not immediately go off. It went off when the trigger came back up. We had a fella that lives in Florida stepped on one. He still lives in Florida. He may have a little trouble walking. He has both his legs and feet, but they don't operate properly. And if you ask him he says he was lucky. He was. He's still here. Usually when you wound up stepping on one and it went off, you went with it. But in his case it just worked out. We cleared mines off beaches in England. Some of those mines had been there for quite some time. We lost two fellas instantly; they found the mine, set about to take it out, and it went off. They both died right there. It happened often. Not as a regular basis but often. Booby traps. Booby traps in themselves never looked like much. There was the other end of it that looked pretty big and usually was. But when it came time to check out a road or a roadway for mines or something, usually they sent the engineers in to see how bad it was. But you never hear about them. When somebody says, "What were you in the service"? I tell them I was a combat engineer. And they say, "An engineer? What the hell is that?" Which is about true. What the hell is that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, I've talked to a couple since I started doing this. I think they were smaller outfits so you just don't hear as much about it, I guess.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Well that smaller outfit, when the infantry or the armored came to a chasm road that's about 30-foot deep and about 60-foot across, that tank is not going to drive over it. So that small outfit was brought up and they built a bridge across that chasm. And then the infantry and the armored raced across it and on into the distant future. When they were through, those engineers took it down again. They built a bridge across the river. A hundred yards up stream and a hundred yards down stream nets were put in, weighted, and tied down and a guard was posted. Not a guard, two or three, to see when the top of the net would move. Water didn't do that. People did that. In between those nets they built a bridge across the river. The other side will do anything to keep you from finishing it. But that was that little unit that doesn't get mentioned that laid out on the end of that thing and laid the floor on it and put the bridge together so that they could go across it and rush onward. I don't know what we'd have done without them but once in a while mention us. We were there. But when they got in a bind and we didn't have the bridge to build or anything else, it was not uncommon to find that engineer laying on the ground alongside the infantry man with his rifle, shooting also. Granted, he didn't get the rifleman's badge, but he was there. The medics are another one; a small outfit. There is a small outfit. They were all over the place. You don't hear too much about them either. I'll give them this much: You do hear more about them than you hear about the engineers. I'm prejudice, of course.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (Laughing) And rightly so.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: But...

sp.speaker: Unidentified female
sp.p: That's why you got that medal.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: I guess. It's -- for a guy that tried to enlist in the service and couldn't make it, I spent almost five years in there. I didn't enjoy every minute of it, but I had a good time. The one thing I can say is I had one advantage over a good number of draftees. I used to spend my summers in Indiana on a farm. And my uncle was a great sportsman; fishing, hunting. He loved to hunt. And he taught me that when you go hunting you hunt for food but not all time. I have gone out with him in the morning out in the pickup truck, drove off, went to where we were going to spend the day; and it is cold out there. Snow's on the ground. And I have walked with him the whole day and he never put his rifle together. Never put it, never straightened the shotgun out. Just walked and talked. And for him that was a great day. Then again I have been with him when we have had our so called limit in three hours. After that we just talked and walked. You don't shoot more than you need. He was great for that. He also taught me how to shoot. You have no idea how many times I have thought about that. That ____, yeah, there's medals but when it came time for discharge I asked if I could stay. And after he looked over my records he says, "Sure. We'll keep you six weeks and give you a medical discharge." "Hell, if you are only going to keep me six weeks, I'll go now." So, I went then. But it was good. Not the easiest days of my life but some of the best.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Good. Any memories of mail call, getting letters from home?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah, we wrote each other before we got married. I use to -- I drove -- when we were overseas I drove our mail officer insane. I used to write on a tablet and stick the pages together on the end.

sp.speaker: Unidentified female
sp.p: Wrote me a seven-page letter -- or a seven-foot long letter.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (Laughing) A seven-foot long letter?

sp.speaker: Unidentified female
sp.p: Yeah, he wrote beautiful.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: But up until that time I had never heard from the officer that read the mail and took out what wasn't suppose to be. After that letter I heard from him. Casually, "Oh, um, Houghtlin, can I see you a minute?" ______ poured in. He says, "This is between you and me." He says, "Don't ever write another letter like that and stick the ends together. Do we understand each other?" And all I could say was, "Yes, sir." So I never stuck another one together. I may have wrote seven page letters, but I never stuck them together again.

sp.speaker: Unidentified female
sp.p: Tell him how about V-mail you sent my mom.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: I sent my mother-in-law -- you have to realize that my time in the service was draft time. And you got anybody and everybody. And my soon to be in-laws were Bohemian Slovock. I couldn't find a Bohemian Slovock but I found a Polock who spoke and wrote and read Polish. So we sent my mother-in-law to be an e-mail in Polish. God love her, she had to go get somebody to read it to her; but it worked out because I didn't write any more of those either. But somewhere here I have a copy of -- I have an e-mail, an actual e-mail in the envelope. I also have the gas ration stamps they used in the states.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, were they able to shrink that 7-page letter down to a v-mail size?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: No. That's when you could still send letters.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, that was when you were still allowed to send regular letters, okay.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Yeah. The v-mail came after that. But, yeah, they found a way to take care of us seven-page letter writers. They issued us a sheet of paper and a small three-by-four envelope that it fit in. But I sent stuff back home from Ireland. And I sent my mother and my future wife a tablecloth on Irish linen. We had ours up until --

sp.speaker: Unidentified female
sp.p: -- about a year ago. It started to disintegrate.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Not surprising. But...

sp.speaker: Unidentified female
sp.p: Beautiful.

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: It was a good life. I enjoyed the men I was with. I'm still friends with some of them. Jimmy Scrohovich (ph) out of Seven Hills. Zluzniak (ph). He lives west of here now. He use to live out in the North Royalton. Got them from all over. But we go to lunch now and then. Now I take my wife and one of the daughters to lunch when I go to lunch with the fellas because I, of course, don't drive anymore. She don't drive anymore. She's having eye trouble. But it was a good life.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: Never resented a minute of it, health problems and all. But that is about the best I can do for you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was your sight loss related to your wound?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: They told me no. I had a doctor in the Veterans Administration VA Hospital system that told my wife and I that I was totally disabled and anything that would happen to me in the future would be offshoot of having my brains rattled. Not so. I do draw disability. I draw it for my brains being scattered and whittled it down to where I have chronic sinusitis. And for that they pay me. Nothing is said about the forehead I lost or the cranial leak that I have been told I still have. But -- or the trips I still make to the VA. But all in all I'm still here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Very good. You think we got it?

sp.speaker: Jack Houghtlin
sp.p: I think so.
